absent: Acquisition, reference counting and install rules for time namespaces beyond owner mapping.
Full layout of time namespace, offsets structure and virtual page lifecycle.
Timekeeper and keeper array structures, cycle to nanosecond conversion, and suspend handling.
NTP scale, shift, interval, phase and frequency limit constants and status and state flag values.
Pulse per second hard update path, background sync work definition, and hardware clock writeback.
Proc file wiring, offset request structure layout, and capability check semantics.
Locking for per keeper NTP data and timer lifecycle beyond the shown callback.

findings.text: Proc display for a task child time namespace emits one row per supported clock, first monotonic then boottime, using stored offsets; it produces no output when the task has no such namespace.

Proc offset installer for a task child time namespace checks presence, capability against the namespace owner, clock identity, seconds and nanoseconds ranges, and resulting wall time bounds, then under a mutex refuses frozen namespaces and otherwise stores all supplied values.
Monotonic time getter fills a caller timespec with seconds plus nanoseconds derived from keeper base seconds, monotonic shift, and current cycle delta, retried for consistency.
Two second resolution getters expose wall seconds and NTP seconds for a keeper index, the wall variant using a fast path on wide builds and a retried read otherwise.
NTP control exports reset a keeper discipline state with a clocksource adjustment, and read back current tick length and pending skew delta.

NTP runtime exports drain intentional phase from adjust and offset trackers, report the next insertion instant only for the core keeper in insertion state, and advance leap and skew state once per second returning a leap marker.
Owner helper maps a generic namespace handle to its owning user namespace for permission checks.

Per keeper discipline record holds tick base and length, state and status words, phase and frequency terms, error bounds, reference time, adjust whole and fractional parts, tick adjustments, next leap instant, plus optional pulse calibration and statistics.
Two namespace operation tables expose the time and time for children views with distinct names but shared install, release and owner helpers and separate acquisition helpers.
Initial time namespace starts with frozen offsets enabled and owned by the initial user namespace, and is registered during early init.

Only monotonic and boottime clocks are accepted for display and update; other identities are rejected for update and labelled as unknown for display, seconds must lie within symmetric large bounds, nanoseconds within a second, and the shifted current time must stay non negative and below half the large bound.
Each keeper starts with a user tick base, sane state, unsynchronised status, small time constant, phase limit error bounds, and no scheduled leap.

Frequency recomputation adds tick, NTP and clocksource adjustments and frequency to a scaled second length then reduces by interval frequency; offset updates apply only under phase lock, clamp and scale the sample, select phase or frequency locked loop mode by elapsed seconds, and bound the result.

Per second bookkeeping increments maximum error up to a limit marking unsynchronised, validates pulse signal, settles opposing offset versus adjust slews directly, then publishes a per tick skew rate with a minimal non zero floor when net phase remains.

Pulse handling has two builds: one maintains shift, count, filter history, base, frequency and error classification with jitter and wander rules, the other leaves those operations empty and reports zeroed calibration fields and a simpler error test.

Hardware clock sync uses an absolute high resolution timer whose callback queues background work and does not rearm; scheduling anchors at the current real second start then adds either the long period or a short retry delay minus the supplied offset.
Time namespace internal header provides a single inclusion guard.

Discipline reset stops pending adjustment, marks unsynchronised, restores error bounds to the phase limit, recomputes tick length, clears phase and skew trackers, disarms leap, and clears pulse state.
Offset installation serialises the frozen check and the store of all entries with a dedicated offset mutex held across that region.
Monotonic and wall second readers sample keeper fields under a sequence counter begin and retry loop to obtain a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.

Leap handling cycles among sane, insertion armed, deletion armed, operation pending and waiting: arming schedules end of day, reaching the instant returns a step marker and advances, withdrawal cancels to sane, and waiting returns to sane once flags clear.
Early boot entry registers the initial time namespace in the namespace tree.
Fault helper for the time virtual page returns the current task namespace page when the mapping belongs to current memory, otherwise warns and yields null to block remote access.
Remote access to the time virtual page through another memory context triggers a warning path and provides no page, so callers must handle null.
Monotonic reads warn when timekeeping is suspended, signalling that the sampled values may be taken in an unusual power state.

Offset installation distinguishes missing namespace, insufficient privilege, bad clock or nanoseconds, out of range seconds or result, and frozen state with distinct failures, and performs validation before taking the lock so frozen is checked last.

Phase drains proceed only when the requested amount and the stored phase share sign, never overshoot zero, top up fractional remainder from whole units, keep whole and fractional adjust parts with matching sign, and return unclaimed remainder for the next tracker.
Day length for leap scheduling is 86400 seconds.
Maximum adjtime slew per tick is 500 microseconds, with a scaled per tick form derived from it, and maximum time authority offset is 100000.
Pulse watchdog is 10 seconds, popcorn threshold shift 4, frequency interval shifts from 2 to 8 with 4 consecutive intervals to move, and maximum wander 100000 nanoseconds per second.
One microsecond in scaled nanoseconds is the nanoseconds per microsecond factor shifted by the NTP scale.
Hardware clock synchronisation period is eleven minutes expressed in nanoseconds, with retry scheduling two seconds past the minute boundary.
